'''William B. Tolman''' (born May 20, 1961, in [[Cleveland]], [[Ohio]]) an American inorganic chemist focusing on the synthesis and characterization of model [[Bioinorganic chemistry|bioinorganic]] systems, and [[Organometallic chemistry|organometallic]] approaches towards [[polymer chemistry]]. He is currently the Al and Mary Agnes McQuinn Distinguished Chair and Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences at the [[University of St. Thomas (Minnesota)]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=William Tolman {{!}} Chemistry |url=https://cas.stthomas.edu/departments/faculty/william-tolman/index.html |access-date=2026-02-08 |website=cas.stthomas.edu |language=en}}</ref> He has served as Editor in Chief of the [[American Chemical Society|ACS]] journal ''[[Inorganic Chemistry (journal)|Inorganic Chemistry]],''<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Elwell|first1=Courtney E.|last2=Gagnon|first2=Nicole L.|last3=Neisen|first3=Benjamin D.|last4=Dhar|first4=Debanjan|last5=Spaeth|first5=Andrew D.|last6=Yee|first6=Gereon M.|last7=Tolman|first7=William B.|date=2017-02-08|title=Copper–Oxygen Complexes Revisited: Structures, Spectroscopy, and Reactivity|journal=Chemical Reviews|volume=117|issue=3|pages=2059–2107|doi=10.1021/acs.chemrev.6b00636|pmid=28103018|pmc=5963733|issn=0009-2665}}</ref> and as a Senior Investigator at the NSF Center for Sustainable Polymers.<ref>{{Cite web|title=William Tolman|url=https://csp.umn.edu/team/william-tolman/|website=NSF Center for Sustainable Polymers (CSP)|access-date=2021-06-03|archive-date=2021-06-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603194151/https://csp.umn.edu/team/william-tolman/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Tolman is a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=Editor-in-Chief|url=https://pubs.acs.org/page/inocaj/profile.html|access-date=2021-06-03|website=pubs.acs.org|language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Tolman was born on May 20, 1961, in [[Cleveland]], but grew up in [[Chelmsford, Massachusetts]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Tolman|first=William B.|year=1997|title=Making and Breaking the Dioxygen O−O Bond: New Insights from Studies of Synthetic Copper Complexes|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|language=en|volume=30|issue=6|pages=227–237|doi=10.1021/ar960052m}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> He received his B.A. in chemistry from [[Wesleyan University]] in 1983, where he conducted organometallic chemistry research with [[Alan Cutler|Alan R. Cutler]].<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-02-18|title=Bill Tolman|url=https://www.aiche.org/community/bio/bill-tolman|access-date=2021-06-03|website=www.aiche.org|language=en}}</ref> With Cutler, Tolman studied the bimetallic activation of coordinated ligands of molybdenum cyclopentadienyl complexes.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1985-10-08|title=Bimetallic activation of coordinated ligands. Reactions of the Lewis acid (η-C5H5)(CO)3Mo+ PF6− with organo-iron and -molybdenum η1-methoxymethyl and ethyl complexes|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0022328X85880529|journal=Journal of Organometallic Chemistry|language=en|volume=294|issue=1|pages=45–58|doi=10.1016/0022-328X(85)88052-9|issn=0022-328X|last1=Markham|first1=James|last2=Tolman|first2=William|last3=Menard|first3=Kevin|last4=Cutler|first4=Alan|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Tolman then moved on to graduate studies at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he worked in the laboratory of Prof. [[Peter Vollhardt|K. Peter C. Vollhardt]] as a W. R. Grace Graduate Fellow.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Tolman Group Laboratory|url=http://www1.chem.umn.edu/groups/tolman/|access-date=2017-06-06|website=www1.chem.umn.edu}}</ref> In Vollhardt's laboratory, Tolman studied [[photochemistry]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Boese|first1=Roland|last2=Cammack|first2=J. Kevin|last3=Matzger|first3=Adam J.|last4=Pflug|first4=Kai|last5=Tolman|first5=William B.|last6=Vollhardt|first6=K. Peter C.|last7=Weidman|first7=Timothy W.|date=1997|title=Photochemistry of (Fulvalene)tetracarbonyldiruthenium and Its Derivatives: Efficient Light Energy Storage Devices|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/ja9707062|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=119|issue=29|pages=6757–6773|doi=10.1021/ja9707062|bibcode=1997JAChS.119.6757B |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and ligand substitution reactions of bimetallic [[coordination complex]]es with the [[Fulvalene|fulvalene ligand]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Boese|first1=Roland|last2=Tolman|first2=William B.|last3=Vollhardt|first3=K. Peter C.|date=1986|title=Carbonyl substitution and ring slippage upon reaction of trialkylphosphines with (fulvalene)diruthenium tetracarbonyl. X-ray structural analysis of (.eta.0:.eta.4-C10H8)Ru(PMe3)2CO and fluxional behavior of (.eta.5:.eta.5-C10H8)Ru2(CO)3L (L = phosphine)|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/om00134a029|journal=Organometallics|volume=5|issue=3|pages=582–584|doi=10.1021/om00134a029|issn=0276-7333|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Huffman|first1=Mark A.|last2=Newman|first2=David A.|last3=Tilset|first3=Mats|last4=Tolman|first4=William B.|last5=Vollhardt|first5=K. Peter C.|date=1986|title=Designed syntheses of heterobimetallic fulvalene complexes|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/om00140a038|journal=Organometallics|volume=5|issue=9|pages=1926–1928|doi=10.1021/om00140a038|issn=0276-7333|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Tolman graduated with a Ph.D. in chemistry in 1987.<ref name=":4" />

He then conducted his postdoc in the laboratory of Prof. [[Stephen J. Lippard]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] with the support of a fellowship from the [[American Cancer Society]]. With Prof. Lippard, Tolman synthesized novel [[ligand]]s for [[coordination complex]]es that model the active sites of [[metalloprotein]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tolman|first1=William B.|last2=Rardin|first2=R. Lynn|last3=Lippard|first3=Stephen J.|date=1989|title=A dinucleating hexaimidazole ligand and its dicopper(II) methanol inclusion complex|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/ja00194a077|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=111|issue=12|pages=4532–4533|doi=10.1021/ja00194a077|bibcode=1989JAChS.111.4532T |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He then synthesized complexes that model [[Non-heme iron protein|nonheme diiron proteins]], and studied their reactivity with [[Oxygen|O<sub>2</sub>]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tolman|first1=William B.|last2=Bino|first2=Avi|last3=Lippard|first3=Stephen J.|date=1989|title=Self assembly and dioxygen reactivity of an asymmetric, triply bridged diiron(II) complex with imidazole ligands and an open coordination site|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/ja00204a037|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=111|issue=22|pages=8522–8523|doi=10.1021/ja00204a037|bibcode=1989JAChS.111.8522T |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tolman|first1=William B.|last2=Liu|first2=Shuncheng|last3=Bentsen|first3=James G.|last4=Lippard|first4=Stephen J.|date=1991|title=Models of the reduced forms of polyiron-oxo proteins: an asymmetric, triply carboxylate bridged diiron(II) complex and its reaction with dioxygen|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/ja00001a023|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=113|issue=1|pages=152–164|doi=10.1021/ja00001a023|bibcode=1991JAChS.113..152T |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Career ==
Tolman began his independent career in 1990, as an assistant professor in the Department of Chemistry at the [[University of Minnesota|University of Minnesota, Twin Cities]] (UMN).<ref name=":4" /> He was appointed a Distinguished McKnight University Professor in 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Honorary professorships {{!}} College {{!}} College of Science and Engineering|url=https://cse.umn.edu/college/honorary-professorships|access-date=2021-06-03|website=cse.umn.edu}}</ref> He previously served as the Chair of the Department of Chemistry at UMN, from 2009 to 2016.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Tolman named chair of Department of Chemistry {{!}} College {{!}} College of Science and Engineering|url=https://cse.umn.edu/college/feature-stories/tolman-named-chair-department-chemistry|access-date=2021-06-03|website=cse.umn.edu}}</ref> In 2018, Tolman moved with his research group to [[Washington University in St. Louis]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|last=Gauen|first=Claire|date=2018-01-10|title=Spring 2018 New Faculty|url=https://artsci.wustl.edu/ampersand/spring-2018-new-faculty|access-date=2021-06-03|website=Washington University in St. Louis - Arts & Sciences|language=en}}</ref> Generally, Tolman's research group works on the synthesis of bioinorganic coordination complexes that model the active sites of metalloproteins, as well as the synthesis of organometallic complexes for the polymerization of cyclic esters.<ref name=":4" />

In the summer of 2022, Tolman became the dean of the College of Arts and Sciences at the [[University of St. Thomas (Minnesota)|University of St. Thomas]], in St. Paul, Minnesota.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ybarra |first=Andy |date=2022-04-07 |title=St. Thomas Appoints Renowned Chemistry Scholar to Lead College of Arts and Sciences |url=https://news.stthomas.edu/new-cas-dean/ |access-date=2022-10-03 |website=Newsroom {{!}} University of St. Thomas |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Copper-oxygen adducts ===
Tolman's work in the bioinorganic field focuses on Cu-O adducts, specifically copper proteins whose diverse, biological functions include: O<sub>2</sub> transport, aromatic ring oxidations, biogenesis of hormones.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Lewis|first1=Elizabeth A.|last2=Tolman|first2=William B.|title=Reactivity of Dioxygen−Copper Systems|journal=Chemical Reviews|language=en|volume=104|issue=2|pages=1047–1076|doi=10.1021/cr020633r|pmid=14871149|year=2004}}</ref>  His work studies the potential of 1:1 Cu/O<sub>2</sub> adducts as catalytic species, which have been known as transient intermediates for more commonly studied 2:1 and even 3:1 Cu/O<sub>2</sub> molecules. These complexes, while kinetically favored in formation are thermodynamically unstable due to negative entropy values, thus making them more difficult to isolate.<ref name=":1" /> Although, increasing ligand sizes on these 1:1 adducts did correlate with slower [[reaction rate]] constants; advantageous for isolating and studying these complexes.<ref name=":0" />
[[File:Copper_Oxygen_Adduct.jpg|thumb|This figure shows copper and oxygen bonded at differing ratios.]]
Furthermore, his work on high and mixed valent copper species including [CuOH]<sup>+2</sup> and its conjugate base, [CuO]<sup>+</sup> is also very notable. His work with [CuOH]<sup>+2</sup> reveals a high reactivity with C-H and O-H bonds as compared to its conjugate acid pair.<ref name=":0" /> This is of importance when trying to replicate biological mechanisms, such as copper-catalyzed oxidation in vitro.

His research has contributed to the discovery and characterization of new biomimetic species. It is his goal to not only identify these compounds, but to comprehensively understand the intermediates and mechanisms with which they play crucial roles in facilitating. In the case of Cu/O<sub>2</sub> adducts, realizing their biological role and function in copper containing enzymes can give rise to new insights on their biomimetic properties.<ref name=":0" />

Additionally, his lab is searching for alternative, synthetic oxidative catalysis. This includes designing biochemically inspired synthetic catalysts as well as trying O<sub>2</sub> as a candidate for controlled, in vitro oxidation. Due to high abundances and relatively strong stabilizing capabilities within biological reactions, iron and copper enzymes inspire biomimetic synthetic catalysts. Although these reactions perform with high accuracy and selectivity within the body, many challenges arise when working with O<sub>2</sub> in vitro because of the undesired and potentially harmful side products that can be generated.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Que|first1=Lawrence|last2=Tolman|first2=William B.|date=2008-09-18|title=Biologically inspired oxidation catalysis|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=455|issue=7211|pages=333–340|doi=10.1038/nature07371|pmid=18800132|bibcode=2008Natur.455..333Q|s2cid=4427860|issn=0028-0836}}</ref>

=== Organometallic polymerization catalysts ===
[[File:LA to PLA-2.jpg|thumb|341x341px|Polymerization of lactide to polylactic acid with a Zn(II) alkoxide catalyst.<ref name=":3" />]]
Tolman's work on organometallic polymerization catalysis focuses on the development of new metal catalysts for the more efficient polymerization of [[Cyclic ester|lactones]] into [[biodegradable polymer]]s. An example of this work is the use of Zn(II) or Fe(III) [[alkoxide]] catalysts, which can polymerize [[lactide]] (LA) into [[polylactic acid]] (PLA).<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=O'Keefe|first1=Brendan J.|last2=Breyfogle|first2=Laurie E.|last3=Hillmyer|first3=Marc A.|last4=Tolman|first4=William B.|title=Mechanistic Comparison of Cyclic Ester Polymerizations by Novel Iron(III)−Alkoxide Complexes: Single vs Multiple Site Catalysis|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=124|issue=16|pages=4384–4393|doi=10.1021/ja012689t|pmid=11960467|year=2002|bibcode=2002JAChS.124.4384O }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Williams|first1=Charlotte K.|last2=Breyfogle|first2=Laurie E.|last3=Choi|first3=Sun Kyung|last4=Nam|first4=Wonwoo|last5=Young|first5=Victor G.|last6=Hillmyer|first6=Marc A.|last7=Tolman|first7=William B.|title=A Highly Active Zinc Catalyst for the Controlled Polymerization of Lactide|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=125|issue=37|pages=11350–11359|doi=10.1021/ja0359512|pmid=16220958|year=2003|bibcode=2003JAChS.12511350W |s2cid=8507612}}</ref> PLA is of great interest because it is both biodegradable and a renewable resource.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ceresana.com/en/market-studies/plastics/bioplastics/|title=Bioplastics - Study: Market, Analysis, Trends {{!}} Ceresana|last=Kuehner|first=Marcel|website=www.ceresana.com|language=en|access-date=2017-06-06}}</ref> While there are many well known catalysts available to synthesize PLA, not much is known about their mechanism of catalysis - this proves problematic in the design of new and more efficient catalysts. Thus, Tolman's group is pursuing the synthesis and characterization of less structurally complex catalysts.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=O'Keefe|first1=Brendan J.|last2=Hillmyer|first2=Marc A.|last3=Tolman|first3=William B.|date=2001-01-01|title=Polymerization of lactide and related cyclic esters by discrete metal complexes|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Dalton Transactions|language=en|issue=15|pages=2215–2224|doi=10.1039/B104197P|issn=1364-5447}}</ref> His research has showed that catalysts with lower [[coordination number]]s have higher polymerization activities.<ref name=":3" /> His Zn(II) alkoxide catalyst, for example, produced PLA with a high molecular weight at a relatively fast rate.

=== Role in Gianluigi Veglia sexual harassment investigation ===
As UMN Chemistry Department Chair in 2017, Tolman was one of four administrators notified about, and provided the results of, an investigation into allegations involving UMN biochemistry and chemistry professor Gianluigi Veglia.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|last1=Widener|first1=Andrea|last2=Wang|first2=Linda|date=March 15, 2021|title=Gianluigi Veglia sexually harassed his students and lab staff but wasn't fired|url=https://cen.acs.org/careers/women-in-science/sexual-harassment-gianluigi-veglia-minnesota-not-fired/99/i9|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210429095332/https://cen.acs.org/careers/women-in-science/sexual-harassment-gianluigi-veglia-minnesota-not-fired/99/i9|archive-date=2021-04-29|access-date=2021-06-06|website=cen.acs.org|publisher=[[Chemical & Engineering News]]}}</ref> Tolman left UMN the following year for a position in the [[Arts and Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis]].<ref name=":6" />

== Awards ==
Tolman is the recipient of many awards for his research, including an [[American Chemical Society|ACS]] [[List of American Chemical Society national awards|Award for Distinguished Service in the Advancement of Inorganic Chemistry]] in 2017,<ref>{{Cite web|title=ACS Award for Distinguished Service in the Advancement of lnorganic Chemistry|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-for-distinguished-service-in-the-advancement-of-lnorganic-chemistry.html|access-date=2021-06-03|website=American Chemical Society|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Wang|first=Linda|date=January 2, 2017|title=ACS Award for Distinguished Service in the Advancement of Inorganic Chemistry: William B. Tolman|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/95/i1/ACS-Award-Distinguished-Service-Advancement.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201023090638/https://cen.acs.org/articles/95/i1/ACS-Award-Distinguished-Service-Advancement.html|archive-date=2020-10-23|access-date=2021-06-03}}</ref> the Charles E. Bowers Teaching Award from the University of Minnesota in 2012,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Honors and Awards - 2012 {{!}} College {{!}} College of Science and Engineering|url=https://cse.umn.edu/college/honors-and-awards-2012|access-date=2021-06-03|website=cse.umn.edu}}</ref> a Alexander von Humboldt Foundation Research Award for 2004–2005,<ref name=":4" /> a Buck-Whitney Medal from the ACS Eastern New York Section in 2001,<ref name=":4" /> a Camille & Henry Dreyfus Teacher–Scholar Award in 1999,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Camille Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar Awards Program|url=https://www.dreyfus.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/camille-past.pdf}}</ref> and a Searle Scholars Award in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web|title=William B. Tolman|url=https://www.searlescholars.net/people/william-b-tolman|access-date=2021-06-03|website=Searle Scholars Program|language=en|archive-date=2021-06-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603194151/https://www.searlescholars.net/people/william-b-tolman|url-status=dead}}</ref>

He was elected a Fellow of the American Chemical Society in 2010,<ref>{{Cite web|title=2010 ACS Fellows|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/fellows/list-of-2010-acs-fellows.html|access-date=2021-06-03|website=American Chemical Society|language=en}}</ref> and a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 2006.<ref>{{Cite web|title=AAAS 2006 Annual Report|url=https://www.aaas.org/sites/default/files/AnnualReports/2006/aaas_annualreport06.pdf}}</ref>
